item.text:
**4B.10: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2024**

Overall judgment: **weaker than inherited.** I found a few partial easing signals in 2024, but the year’s main pattern was continued repression, weak due process, and no meaningful expansion of political freedom or democratic resilience.

**Accepted claims**
- **Sisi ordered implementation of National Dialogue recommendations on pretrial detention and alternatives** | Presidency of the Republic of Egypt | 2024-08-21 | [URL](https://www.presidency.eg/EN/%D9%82%D8%B3%D9%85_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%AE%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%B1/%D8%A3%D8%AE%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%B1-%D8%B1%D8%A6%D8%A7%D8%B3%D9%8A%D8%A9/news2182024/) | This is the strongest official positive signal: Sisi told the government to reduce maximum pretrial detention and implement alternatives. It is real procedural easing, but it is narrow and does not show a broad democratic opening. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.4, 4B.5
- **Authorities closed Case 173 and lifted some travel bans, but asset freezes and charges persisted** | Human Rights Watch | 2024-07-15 | [URL](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/07/15/human-rights-watch-submission-universal-periodic-review-egypt) | HRW says the March 2024 closure of Case 173 and gradual lifting of some travel bans were partial relief measures. HRW also stresses that many activists still faced asset freezes and terrorism charges, so this was limited easing, not systemic resilience. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.3, 4B.4, 4B.5
- **Alaa Abdel Fattah was released on a presidential pardon in September 2024** | Amnesty International | 2024-09-22 | [URL](https://www.amnesty.org/en/location/middle-east-and-north-africa/egypt/report-egypt/) | Amnesty notes the activist’s release under pardon. This is a genuine, but isolated, positive signal on political prisoners and does not amount to a durable improvement in political freedom. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.3, 4B.5
- **Freedom House says Egypt remained “Not Free” and Sisi’s third term followed an election marked by arrests and intimidation** | Freedom House | 2024 | [URL](https://freedomhouse.org/country/egypt/freedom-world/2024) | Freedom House’s 2024 assessment shows no meaningful change from the inherited authoritarian baseline: opposition remained virtually nonexistent, civil liberties stayed tightly restricted, and the election that produced the term was noncompetitive. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.3, 4B.4, 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.7, 4B.8
- **HRW said the crackdown on civic space continued and national dialogue produced no recognizable reforms** | Human Rights Watch | 2024-01-11 | [URL](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/egypt-civic-space-under-siege) | HRW described a heavy crackdown on free expression and assembly ahead of the vote, with arrests and detentions used to intimidate participation. That points to democratic resilience getting worse, not better. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.3, 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.9
- **HRW said Sisi’s rule had violently quashed dissent and left basic freedoms worse than before** | Human Rights Watch | 2024-02-26 | [URL](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/02/26/egypts-al-sisi-has-caged-himself) | HRW’s synthesis is blunt: Sisi’s government had crushed dissent and hollowed out basic freedoms, with promises of prosperity failing to translate into resilience. This is strong negative evidence on the inherited baseline comparison. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.3, 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.9
- **Amnesty said the new criminal procedure code would entrench abusive detention and empower prosecutors** | Amnesty International | 2024-10-02 | [URL](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/10/egypt-reject-draft-criminal-procedure-code/) | Amnesty and partner groups argued the draft code failed to curb abusive pretrial detention and instead entrenched prosecutorial discretion. That is evidence of institutional weakening, not democratic resilience. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.4, 4B.5, 4B.9
- **HRW said rights defenders, journalists, and activists still faced travel bans, asset freezes, and prosecutions** | Human Rights Watch | 2024-07-15 | [URL](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/07/15/human-rights-watch-submission-universal-periodic-review-egypt) | Even where some bans were lifted, HRW says the broader system of judicial and security harassment remained. That means the state did not leave civil society stronger than it found it. | QIDs: 4B.10, 4B.3, 4B.4, 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.9

**Search gap**
- I found **some** limited positive procedural moves in 2024, especially on pretrial detention and a few political-prisoner cases.
- I found **no evidence** of a broad, durable strengthening of political freedom or democratic resilience.
- The best-supported reading is that 2024 left Egypt **at least as repressive, and likely more constrained in practice**, than the system Sisi inherited.
